paras: The expulsion notice to the Dabney brothers was an order given in December 1903 by citizens of Port Royal, Caroline County, Virginia, that a Black man named Dabney and his brothers leave the county within twenty-four hours, after they fell under suspicion in a night attack on a young physician, Dr. Lloyd Norland. The men disappeared, and within about two weeks three brothers named Walker, reported as the suspected attackers, had been arrested, jailed at Bowling Green and sent on to a grand jury. Fredericksburg and Richmond papers mentioned the notice in a single sentence, as a step the citizens took because no direct evidence could be found.

Norland, whose name a later Richmond dispatch spelled Noland, was a young physician at Port Royal whom the Times-Dispatch called "prominent" and connected to Richmond families. According to the Fredericksburg reports, he had earlier had "a difficulty with a negro whose name is Dabney," though no paper described that dispute.

One night in early December, someone called Norland to the door of his office and, as he opened it, struck him a "stunning blow" on the head that threw him into the street. He made his way toward the hotel about fifty yards off and fired his revolver to draw help before losing consciousness, and two physicians worked on him until nearly morning. Norland did not know who had struck him but said he had seen a Black man in an ulster overcoat across the street, and half a brick found on the step was supposed to have been the weapon.

Suspicion fell on Dabney and, in the Times-Dispatch version, two of his brothers, but the Free Lance reported that "no direct evidence could be obtained." "The citizens took the matter up," the Free Lance wrote, by giving the men notice that they must leave the county in twenty-four hours. The men then disappeared, and Sheriff Gill went after them in the belief that they had gone to King George County.

On or about Monday, December 14, Charles and Woody Walker, two of three brothers "supposed to be" the attackers, were taken at Stiff's Wharf on the Potomac in King George County as they prepared to board a steamer for Washington. Constable J. B. King of Shiloh and a deputy made the arrest and carried the prisoners through King George to the Caroline County jail at Bowling Green. A third brother, named Jeff, Judd or Judge Walker in different reports, was arrested in Washington and brought to Bowling Green by Sheriff T. B. Gill on a charge of assault with intent to kill.

A Port Royal dispatch credited a Richmond National Detective Agency operative with tracing the third brother and gathering the evidence. After a preliminary hearing before two Caroline County magistrates, the brothers were held without bail for the circuit court grand jury due to meet on January 11, 1904, and the prosecutor, Delegate Bernard Powers, said there was "ample evidence to convict." By then Norland was reported to be making fair progress toward recovery, and no report of the grand jury's action or of a trial was found in the coverage.

The coverage found came entirely from white papers in Virginia and Washington, led by the Fredericksburg Free Lance, which followed the case in four items between December 15 and 24; no Black-press report was found. A Fredericksburg special dated December 14 ran in the Richmond Times-Dispatch under the headline "Blow from Dark May Prove Fatal," and the Virginia Gazette of Williamsburg reprinted it on January 2, 1904, as "Struck at His Own Door." Both Fredericksburg accounts placed the citizens' notice in a single sentence between the attack and the sheriff's search, neither praising nor criticizing it.

Later items dropped the notice and followed the case as a police matter, with the Washington Evening Star recording the Walker arrests in its port news column. The Times-Dispatch's Port Royal dispatch, headlined "All Three Run Down," called the attack a "murderous assault" by "three negroes" and named the jailed brothers the "Assailants of Dr. Noland" before any trial.

The reports differ on the date of the attack: the Free Lance of December 15 placed it "last Wednesday night," while the later Port Royal dispatch gave the night of December 6. The first reports named the suspect as Dabney, while every later report concerned brothers surnamed Walker, and no article explains the difference.

accounts.gist: Norland was struck by an unknown person; suspicion fell on Dabney and his brothers without direct evidence, and citizens gave them twenty-four hours to leave the county before the sheriff took up the case.

accounts.label: Port Royal special (prosecution side)
accounts.gist: The 'murderous assault' was committed by three negroes; a detective gathered evidence against the three Walker brothers, and the prosecutor considered it ample to convict.

framing.detail: The Free Lance headlined 'Dr. Norland Assaulted' and reported that 'the citizens took the matter up' with a twenty-four-hour notice, without comment.
Times-Dispatch Fredericksburg special 'Blow from Dark May Prove Fatal' reported the notice in one sentence among local items.
Arrest items ('Arrested', 'Judd Walker Arrested in Washington', Evening Star port column) followed the case as a police matter and did not mention the notice.
Times-Dispatch 'All Three Run Down' called the arrested men 'Assailants of Dr. Noland' and praised the detective's work before any trial; it did not mention the notice.
Virginia Gazette reprinted the Fredericksburg special as 'Struck at His Own Door'.
